segments: "Branching is Git’s killer feature. It is extremely lightweight and encourages you to create a branch for every small idea."
1. Basic branch operations
Building on Git 00, a branch is simply a “pointer.”
Creating and switching
Listing and deleting
2. Two modes of merging: Merge
When you merge the feature branch back into master, Git chooses its approach based on the topology of the commit history.
A. Fast-forward merge
If master has no new commits since the branches diverged, Git simply moves the pointer forward.
Characteristics: No new merge commit is created, and the history remains perfectly linear.
B. Three-way merge

When both sides have diverged, Git performs a three-way merge using their common ancestor and the content at both tips. On successful completion, it creates a merge commit. The commonly used strategy for two-head merges today is ort; recursive, as seen in older material, is not a generic name for three-way merging.
Advanced: Forcing a merge commit (--no-ff)

Why is this useful?: A fast-forward loses the information that “a feature branch existed here.” In practice, we often use git merge --no-ff feature/example to force that branch history to remain visible, making later code audits easier.
3. Resolving conflicts: When Git cannot decide
Git stops and asks you to resolve conflicts when overlapping content cannot be merged automatically. Modify/delete and rename operations can also conflict; conflicts are not limited to the same line.
Conflict markers
Git inserts markers into conflicting files:
Resolution steps
Edit manually: Remove the markers and keep the code you want.
Mark as resolved: Run git add <file> to tell Git that the conflict is resolved.
Complete the merge: Run git commit.
4. Saving work in progress: git stash
Scenario: You are developing a feature when an urgent bug requires switching branches, but your current code is unfinished.
5. Branching strategies: Merge vs. Rebase
This is one of Git’s most enduring debates. The details of using Rebase are covered in Git 04, but it is important to understand the difference in philosophy here.
Property
Merge
Rebase
Underlying logic
Only moves a reference during a fast-forward; otherwise, it can create a merge point.
“Replays” changes from the current branch on top of the target branch.
View of history
Faithfulness: Records the exact point where branches came together.
Tidiness: History is a straight line, as though it never diverged.
Conflict resolution
Resolve all conflicts in one merge.
Each replayed commit may require conflict resolution.
Suitable uses
Team collaboration and public branches.
Personal branches, cleaning up commit history, and staying up to date with upstream.
6. Feature branching workflow
Core principles:
Make keeping master/main usable a team goal: Do not develop directly on it.
One branch per feature: feature/login, fix/issue-101.
Review before merging: When master is ahead, merge its changes into the feature branch to ensure the feature branch is healthy before merging it back into the mainline.
Limits of saving work in progress

A regular stash saves tracked changes in the working tree and index; -u also includes untracked files, while ignored files need separate consideration. You can first use git stash apply to inspect the restored changes, then explicitly run git stash drop. If you need to restore the original staged state, check when --index is applicable. Check the current state before merging, switching, or deleting branches; branch -D deletes a reference that could be used for recovery, but does not delete all old objects.
